snapshots.title: Snapshots
snapshots.intent: A Re-Origination proc converts your stats for 10 seconds. A Tigereye Brew spent inside the proc keeps those stats for the brew's full 15 seconds, so they last well past the proc itself. Catching the procs matters most; catching them late matters less.

snapshots.verdict_ok: {{caught}} of {{total}} catchable procs taken ({{rate, percent}}). You lost more by skipping procs than by brewing late on the ones you took.
snapshots.verdict_bad: {{caught}} of {{total}} catchable procs taken ({{rate, percent}}). This is the spec's largest single source of damage, and most of it was missed.
snapshots.verdict_none: No Re-Origination proc arrived with enough Tigereye Brew banked to be worth spending on, so there was nothing to catch.
snapshots.depth_good: On average you brewed {{depth, percent}} of the way into the proc — late in the window, which extends the buff the longest.
snapshots.depth_ok: On average you brewed {{depth, percent}} of the way in. Waiting until the last global would extend each snapshot further.
snapshots.depth_bad: On average you brewed {{depth, percent}} of the way in, so most of the proc was already over before the brew locked the stats in.

snapshots.b2b_other: {{count}} procs arrived while a snapshotted brew was still running, so part of each could not be used.
snapshots.givenAway: About {{seconds, seconds}} of proc time went unused across the pull.
snapshots.depthCaveat: Depth is averaged over the procs you caught, not the whole pull, so it is shown but never graded — on the pulls used for calibration, catching two procs and timing both perfectly scored better than catching twelve.
snapshots.protected_one: One brew went out early with the bank close to full. Waiting until the last global would have lost {{stacks}} more stacks at the cap, and that would have cost more than the proc time this brew gave up — so it counts as a deliberate choice, not a mistake.
snapshots.protected_other: {{count}} brews went out early with the bank close to full. Waiting until the last global would have lost more stacks at the cap than the proc time they gave up, so they count as deliberate choices, not mistakes.
snapshots.tradeMethod: The comparison is made in stacks and seconds, both ways. Brewing early gives up seconds of a fifteen-second buff carrying the proc's stats; waiting gives up whatever the bank overflows in the meantime, and each lost stack would have amplified a later brew for its whole fifteen seconds. The larger of the two is what this report calls the mistake.
snapshots.tradeNoMastery: What either side is worth in damage depends on your mastery, and WarcraftLogs does not report one on Mists logs — the field exists but always reads zero. So the trade is weighed in stacks and seconds, and no damage number is given.
snapshots.unaffordable_one: One more proc arrived with too few stacks banked to be worth a brew, so it is not counted as a chance missed.
snapshots.unaffordable_other: {{count}} more procs arrived with too few stacks banked to be worth a brew, so they are not counted as chances missed.
snapshots.narrowlyMissed_one: One of the misses was a brew {{ms, gap}} too late — you saw the proc but reacted late.
snapshots.narrowlyMissed_other: {{count}} of the misses were brews that went out just after the proc expired rather than just before, which is a timing problem and not a habit.
snapshots.oneStat: Every proc converted into {{stat}}. The Rune turns your two lowest stats of crit, haste and mastery into twice your highest, so {{stat}} ends up on top of your character sheet. If that is not the stat you want doubled, change the order — reforge, or use an elixir during the fight that lifts another stat above it.
snapshots.weaved_one: One proc came back as {{stat}} instead of {{held}}, because you swapped an elixir right after using the brew. Tigereye Brew freezes your mastery at the moment it is cast, so that proc was never possible to snapshot. It counts as a deliberate play rather than a missed chance, and is left out of the total above.
snapshots.weaved_other: {{count}} procs came back as a stat the running brew could not hold, because an elixir was swapped in right after each brew. Tigereye Brew freezes your mastery at the moment it is cast, so none of them was possible to snapshot. They count as deliberate plays rather than missed chances, and are left out of the total above.

chiBrew.title: Chi Brew
chiBrew.intent: Chi Brew has two charges that recharge every forty-five seconds, and each press gives two chi plus two Tigereye Brew stacks. It can go wrong in two opposite ways: pressing it onto a full chi bar wastes the chi, and never pressing it leaves both charges full and not recharging. The two mistakes are counted separately.
chiBrew.notTalented: You did not take Chi Brew, so there is nothing to report. This is read from the talent list in your log, not from whether the button was pressed — a talent you chose not to take is not a cooldown you forgot to use.
chiBrew.unknownTalent: This log has no character snapshot, so the report cannot tell whether you took Chi Brew. It is not saying you skipped it — it just does not know.
chiBrew.never: You took Chi Brew and never pressed it. While you had something to hit, there was room for about {{possible}} uses, each worth two chi and two brew stacks.
chiBrew.gained_clean: {{uses}} presses of a possible {{possible}}, returning {{gained}} chi, all of which fit on the bar.
chiBrew.gained_wasted: {{uses}} presses of a possible {{possible}}, returning {{gained}} chi — but {{wasted}} of it landed on a full bar and was lost. Chi Brew gives two chi at once, so pressing it above two chi wastes part of the gain.

chiBrew.capped_some: Both charges sat full for {{seconds, duration}} of the time you had something to hit — {{pct, percent}} of that time, worth about {{chi, decimal}} chi. Time when nothing could be hit is not counted against you. The cost is measured in chi rather than presses, because an unused recharge is only part of a press.
chiBrew.scope: Nothing here is graded: the priority list presses Chi Brew when chi is needed and holds it otherwise, and it sets no number of acceptable idle seconds. Charges recharge every {{seconds}}.

debuff.title: Rising Sun Kick
debuff.intent: The debuff increases the damage of everything you and your Storm, Earth and Fire clones do to that target — it does not affect the rest of the raid. It lasts 15 seconds on an 8-second cooldown, so only a missed global can let it drop. Uptime asks whether the enemy you were hitting had the debuff, measured against the time you had something to hit — so add waves and phases with nothing in reach never count against you.

chi.title: Chi
chi.intent: Chi waste is a different mistake from energy waste. Energy fills up on its own whether you press anything or not; chi is only wasted when you press a generator while the bar has no room for what it gives back. Every wasted point below cost you a global.

chi.resolution: This bar is reconstructed, not read directly: WarcraftLogs only reports your chi when you spend it, so the figures come from replaying the log forward through what each button gives and costs. That has two consequences. A point gained and spent between two readings is invisible, so treat the waste shown here as a minimum rather than a total. And spent can exceed gained, because chi you were holding before the log started is paid out here but never counted in.

method.title: Method
method.intent: What was measured and what could not be.
method.engaged: Uptime is measured against engaged time — the pull minus intermissions and time with no target — rather than the raw fight length.
method.energy: Energy is read from the `classResources` snapshot WarcraftLogs stamps onto casts and hits, about three readings a second — not from `resourcechange` events, of which a pull carries around twenty. It is used for time at the cap and nothing else.
method.spec: Classic logs report spec as 0, so the spec is taken from the report's own player list and confirmed by a Tigereye Brew cast.
method.source: One event fetch for report {{code}}, fight {{fightID}}, actor {{actorID}}, straight from your browser to WarcraftLogs.
method.brewStacks: Tigereye Brew stacks are read off the bank aura's removal event, never off the cast — WarcraftLogs logs the drain about a millisecond before the cast, so sampling at the cast reads a bank that has already been spent.
method.dps: DPS is WarcraftLogs' own damage total over the full fight duration.

karma.intent: Touch of Karma redirects the damage you take onto the target for 10 seconds — a defensive ability that also does damage, so an unused charge costs you both. What makes a use good is not when the cooldown came up, but whether anything was actually hitting you while it was running.
karma.verdict_good: {{casts}} of {{available}} uses taken, returning {{reflected, compact}} damage — {{share, percent}} of everything you did. Every press ran while damage was actually coming in.
karma.verdict_ok: {{casts}} of {{available}} uses taken, returning {{reflected, compact}} damage — {{share, percent}} of everything you did. Only part of their potential came back: the redirect only returns damage that hits you while it is running, so timing matters more than the number of uses.
karma.verdict_bad: {{casts}} of {{available}} uses taken, returning {{reflected, compact}} damage — {{share, percent}} of everything you did. Those presses returned far less than they were worth: the redirect only returns damage that hits you while it is running, so time it for when damage is coming in, not for when the cooldown comes up.
karma.verdict_none: Touch of Karma was never pressed, and the pull allowed {{available}} uses.
karma.empty_one: One press redirected nothing at all — a ninety-second cooldown and a global used while nothing was hitting you.
karma.empty_other: {{count}} presses redirected nothing at all — that many ninety-second cooldowns and globals used while nothing was hitting you.
karma.none: Touch of Karma was never pressed, and the pull allowed {{available}} uses.
karma.caption: Every Touch of Karma, and what the redirect returned while it ran
karma.capSummary_one: One use drained its pool completely, which tells us the pool's size: {{health, compact}} health. That is the most one press can absorb, so your {{casts}} uses could have absorbed {{possible, compact}} between them and returned {{absorbed, compact}} — {{pct, percent}} of it.
karma.capSummary_other: {{count}} uses drained their pool completely, which tells us the pool's size: {{health, compact}} health. That is the most one press can absorb, so your {{casts}} uses could have absorbed {{possible, compact}} between them and returned {{absorbed, compact}} — {{pct, percent}} of it.
karma.capUnknown: How much these presses left unspent cannot be said on this pull. Touch of Karma absorbs at most a full health pool, and the only thing that states your pool is a use that drains it — none here did. Guessing from a bar that only reports whole percent would be a guess, not a measurement.
karma.fortifying_one: One of them ran under Fortifying Brew.
karma.fortifying_other: {{count}} of them ran under Fortifying Brew.
karma.fortifyingNote: That is not extra damage. Fortifying Brew raises your maximum health by a fifth, which raises the ceiling on what the redirect can return, and it also cuts the damage you take by a fifth, which is what fills the pool — so only a use already at its ceiling gains anything. The brew does pair with Touch of Death, which rolls against your maximum health; the standard opener casts those two back to back.

xuen.intent: Xuen fights alongside you for 45 seconds on a three-minute cooldown, and the rotation presses it the moment it is ready — nothing else gates it. So the only questions here are how often the tiger was summoned and how much of the fight it was active.

xuen.apl: There is nothing to line it up with: the rotation casts it on cooldown with no condition at all, so using it as soon as it is ready is the entire standard.

sef.title: Storm, Earth and Fire
sef.intent: Each press sends a spirit onto an enemy of your choosing, up to two at a time, and it mirrors your damaging abilities onto that enemy. While they are out your own damage is cut — to 60% with one spirit, 45% with two. So it is only worth pressing when there is a second thing to put a spirit on, and once a spirit is out, the only way to waste it is to attack an enemy that the spirit is already on.
sef.summary_one: {{count}} spirit sent out, out for {{uptime, percent}} of the pull.
sef.summary_other: {{count}} spirits sent out, with at least one of them out for {{uptime, percent}} of the pull.
sef.uptimeMeans: Spirit uptime is the share of the pull, timer to kill, with at least one spirit out. It is not a target to push to 100%, and it cannot tell one spirit from two. A stretch with one enemy calls for no spirit at all, and this figure counts none of that either way. What the pull actually called for is described in the sentence below about second targets.
sef.prePlaced_one: One spirit was already out when the pull began, placed before the timer started, so it spent no global inside the pull and has no cast row. That is an ordinary opener, not a missing press, and it counts here because the spirit was genuinely out. The press that aimed it is outside this log, so its target is worked out from where it swung.
sef.prePlaced_other: {{count}} spirits were already out when the pull began, placed before the timer started, so they spent no globals inside the pull and have no cast rows. That is an ordinary opener, not missing presses, and they count here because the spirits were genuinely out. The presses that aimed them are outside this log, so their targets are worked out from where they swung.
sef.skipped: Storm, Earth and Fire was never pressed, and this pull held a second enemy for {{justified, duration}} in stretches long enough to be worth one — the longest running {{longest, duration}}. Spirits could have been on other enemies during that time.
sef.damage: The spirits dealt {{damage, compact}} between them, {{share, percent}} of your damage — already inside your total, because WarcraftLogs files a pet's damage under its owner.
sef.overlap: For {{overlap, duration}} of your {{measured, duration}} in melee with the spirits out — {{share, percent}} — you were hitting an enemy one of your own spirits already had. That is the damage penalty of a clone copying you onto the same enemy instead of spreading you out.
sef.overlapWorst: The worst of it was {{target}}, at {{ms, duration}}.
sef.overlapNone: You never shared a target with your own spirits.
sef.overlapUnknown: This pull cannot say whether you shared a target with your own spirits: the log carried no separate actor for them, so there is nothing to compare against. The log does not contain enough data to report a figure.
sef.justified: The pull held a second enemy for {{justified, duration}} in stretches longer than {{rule, duration}}, so pressing it was called for.
sef.unjustified: The pull never held a second enemy for longer than {{rule, duration}}; the longest stretch was {{longest, duration}}. Using it against one target is a pure damage loss.
sef.notGraded: Nothing here reaches your score, and the tiles carry no colour except one. The shared-target tile is a reading aid rather than a verdict: the rotation never puts a spirit on the enemy you are hitting, so zero is the mechanic's own answer, not a bar someone set. It is not graded because a strict zero would blame the seconds after your target dies, when you move onto an enemy a spirit is already on.

gear.title: Gear
gear.intent: What you were wearing, straight from the log. Item level is here to be read, not judged. The enchants are the part worth acting on: an empty slot costs damage on every pull until it is filled.
gear.none: This log carried no equipment record, so there is nothing to show. Nothing is wrong with the pull — the report was simply not given the data.

raidBuffs.title: Raid buffs
raidBuffs.intent: The buffs that move a Windwalker's damage, one row per effect rather than one per spell — five classes bring the same attack power and they do not stack, so what matters is whether the effect was on you, not who supplied it. Uptime here is measured against the whole pull, unlike Rising Sun Kick above: a buff stays up perfectly well while the boss is untargetable.
raidBuffs.none: This report was produced before raid buffs were read, so there is nothing to show here. Nothing is wrong with the pull.
raidBuffs.caption: Raid buffs affecting this Windwalker, by effect

worth.stats: Agility is attack power and critical strike at once, which makes this the broadest of the six.
worth.attackPower: A flat multiplier on everything you hit with. Ten percent, not the five it is often quoted as.
worth.meleeHaste: It only speeds up auto-attacks. It does not feed your energy bar, whatever the tooltip suggests.
worth.spellHaste: It shortens the Fists of Fury channel and gives that time back to the rotation. It does not affect energy regeneration — that runs off haste rating from gear.
worth.crit: Flat critical strike chance, and the one most likely to be missing without anyone noticing.
worth.mastery: Flat rating, so what it is worth to you depends on how you have reforged.

raidBuffs.late: Not up at the pull — it went out {{seconds, seconds}} in.
raidBuffs.gaps_other: Off you {{count}} times, for {{seconds, seconds}} in total.
raidBuffs.notReportedNote: {{buffs}} produced no entry in this log at all. That is not the same as missing, so it is not shown as zero: a buff applied before the pull that never drops emits no event all fight, and the log's own snapshot at the pull is not a complete list. The honest answer is that the log did not say — your raid's buff assignments are the place to check.
raidBuffs.self_one: {{buffs}} is one you supply yourself, and it was not up for the whole pull. That is the one row on this page you can fix alone.
raidBuffs.self_other: {{buffs}} are yours to supply, and they were not up for the whole pull. Those are the rows on this page you can fix alone.
raidBuffs.deaths_one: You died once in this pull. You have no buffs while dead, so a gap that lines up with the death is not a missing buff.
raidBuffs.deaths_other: You died {{count}} times in this pull. You have no buffs while dead, so gaps that line up with those deaths are not missing buffs.
raidBuffs.excluded: Stamina and spell power are left out on purpose. Both are real raid buffs and neither adds a point of Windwalker damage, so a row for either would be one nobody can act on.
raidBuffs.debuffs: The two target debuffs a melee cares about — weakened armour and physical vulnerability — are not on this page, and not because they were missing in the raid. The fetch is scoped to you, so a debuff another raider puts on the boss is in neither what you cast nor what was cast on you. Reading them would take a second query this report does not make uninvited.

rotation.title: The rotation
rotation.intent: This is the priority list that every section above compares you against. Nothing here is graded and none of it is about your pull — it is the reference to check when a number looks wrong.
rotation.economy: Two things shape the list. Your global cooldown is a flat second — haste never shortens it, because none of these is a spell; haste buys energy instead. And chi comes slower than globals: Jab costs 40 energy for 2 chi, and energy refills at about ten a second, so a global earns you two thirds of a chi. Two presses in three have to be chi-free. The rest is about caps. Energy caps at 100 and the bank at 20, and nine entries do nothing but keep energy from overcapping. A full bar earns you nothing.

flow.title: The priority flow
flow.intent: Read down the list and press the first thing that is true. There is no separate list for packs — the same rungs apply at one enemy and at six; only how far down the list you get changes.
flow.caption: The priority list, in the order the rotation checks it
flow.reading_single: This is the list at one enemy, which is how the report is reading your pull. Rungs that need two or more enemies are not drawn, and split rungs show only the half that applies. The chips above still name every count where something changes — the control at the top switches the reading.
flow.reading_multi: This is the list at three enemies, the count every press above is judged at. The low-count half of each split rung is not drawn, and neither is the Spinning Crane Kick that needs four. The chips above still name every count where something changes — the control at the top switches the reading.

legend.title: How to read it
legend.spine: Every rung is one question. Yes: press the button beside it and stop there. No: follow the line down to the next question.
legend.gate: A chip across the line is a gate: below the count on it, the question underneath is never asked.
legend.fork: A dashed box is one question with two or three answers. Only one is ever yours, and the line above says what decides.

crossover.title: Where the pack changes the button
crossover.sck: 3+ · Crane Kick over Fists of Fury
crossover.sckOverRsk: 4+ · Crane Kick over Rising Sun Kick

tigereyeBrew.title: Do you have the Rune of Re-Origination?
tigereyeBrew.detail: One button, two rule sets; which one applies depends on whether you have the trinket. A stack costs three chi and a brew spends ten, so the bank fills slowly — the branches disagree only about whether anything is worth waiting for.

talent.title: Which of the three you took
talent.detail: One talent row, so only one of these is ever on your bar. All three do the same job: a global that costs neither chi nor energy, taken only when the bar has room to spare. Their order never matters, because you can only have one.

blackoutKick.title: How much the dump has to leave behind
blackoutKick.detail: One entry with two energy reserves in it, and the number of enemies decides between them: how much has to stay in the bar depends on what else there is to spend it on.

risingSunKick.title: Whether the pack has pushed the kick down the list
risingSunKick.detail: One entry with two halves, and the target count decides which applies — but only from two enemies up. At one the entry is skipped outright and the kick drops to its unconditional rung further down. At two it is pressed on cooldown. From three, the buttons above it beat one kick, and only the debuff running out still triggers this rung.

touchOfDeath.name: Touch of Death
touchOfDeath.test: the target's health drops below yours
touchOfDeath.when: the target's health falls below yours.
touchOfDeath.why: It deals a lump equal to your own maximum health, for one global. The list presses Fortifying Brew in the same breath, because that raises the number it rolls against.

chiBrew.name: Chi Brew
chiBrew.test: 2 chi below cap, in the opener or under a brew
chiBrew.when: you are two chi below the cap, during the opener or with a brew running and energy at least four seconds from full.
chiBrew.why: Two chi for no global. Those two chi save you a Jab, and a Jab you skip is 40 energy left in a bar that was already close to full.

tigereyeBrewRune.name: Tigereye Brew
tigereyeBrewRune.test: a proc is a global from ending and the bank beats it
tigereyeBrewRune.when: the Re-Origination proc is a global from ending and the bank holds more than the buff you are already wearing. Failing that: at a full 20 stacks, above 15 with no proc running, or with the fight ending inside the buff.
tigereyeBrewRune.why: With the Rune on, the brew is a snapshot tool and little else. It reads your mastery once and holds it fifteen seconds, so spending it on the proc's last global is what makes the proc's stats outlive the proc — see below. Every other condition stops the bank overflowing while it waits.

tigereyeBrewBank.name: Tigereye Brew
tigereyeBrewBank.test: no brew running and the bank is at 19
tigereyeBrewBank.when: no brew is already running and the bank is at 19. Below that it wants two chi in hand as well: from 15, from 8 under an agility trinket, from 7 in the opener, or at any size with under 30 seconds left.
tigereyeBrewBank.why: With nothing to snapshot, the only failure left is overflow: 20 is the ceiling, and every stack earned past it is three chi spent for nothing. The two chi is a floor on the state you spend it in — fifteen seconds of buff are worth less off an empty bar.

energizingBrew.name: Energizing Brew
energizingBrew.when: energy is at least five seconds from full. Held through Bloodlust, unless you have Rushing Jade Wind and more than one target.
energizingBrew.why: Sixty energy poured into a nearly full bar is sixty energy gone. Bloodlust already refills the bar faster than a flat one-second global can empty it, so the two overlap into waste.

invokeXuen.name: Invoke Xuen
invokeXuen.why: Nothing. It is the only entry with no condition at all, so the only cost of holding it is a summon that never fits into the fight.

risingSunKickCooldown.name: Rising Sun Kick
risingSunKickCooldown.test: there is a second enemy, and the cooldown is up
risingSunKickCooldown.when: there is exactly one other enemy. Then the rung has no further condition: press it off cooldown. At one enemy the entry is not read at all and the kick waits for its unconditional rung further down.
risingSunKickCooldown.why: The debuff, not the kick — see below. It is the only button here that makes everything else you press hit harder, and a second enemy is what makes it worth a rung this high.

risingSunKickHold.name: Rising Sun Kick
risingSunKickHold.test: its debuff is a global from expiring
risingSunKickHold.when: the debuff it leaves is a global from expiring. From three enemies that is the only thing that claims this rung; otherwise the kick waits for its unconditional rung further down.
risingSunKickHold.why: Holding the debuff, not landing the kick. From three targets the buttons above hit the whole pack and beat one kick, so the list lets it slide — but never far enough to drop the 20% it is lifting everything by.

tigerPalmRefresh.name: Tiger Palm
tigerPalmRefresh.test: Tiger Power has a second or less left
tigerPalmRefresh.when: Tiger Power has a second or less left on it.
tigerPalmRefresh.why: Tiger Power ignores 30% of the target's armour for 20 seconds. It does not stack, so pressing with a healthy buff up throws the rest of it away and takes a global Jab wanted.

chiWave.name: Chi Wave
chiWave.test: cooldown up, energy a second from full
chiWave.when: the 15-second cooldown is up and energy is at least a second from full.
chiWave.why: It costs nothing, which is the problem: a global that generates no energy, spent while the bar is about to cap, is a Jab you could not afford to skip.

zenSphere.name: Zen Sphere
zenSphere.test: cooldown up, energy spare, under two spheres
zenSphere.when: the 10-second cooldown is up, energy is more than two seconds from full, and fewer than two spheres are out. Past two targets it is skipped here and picked up again below Jab, where only the two-sphere limit is left.
zenSphere.why: Two spheres is the cap, so a third press replaces one still ticking. Its energy check is twice Chi Wave's — two seconds of headroom, not one — which is why it sits at a lower rung.

chiBurst.name: Chi Burst
chiBurst.test: cooldown up, energy a global from full
chiBurst.when: the 30-second cooldown is up and energy is more than a global from full.
chiBurst.why: The same check as Chi Wave and the same reason for it, on twice the cooldown: half as many presses over a pull, so half as much to lose by holding one.

comboBreakerKick.name: Blackout Kick
comboBreakerKick.test: Combo Breaker has made it free
comboBreakerKick.when: Combo Breaker has made it free.
comboBreakerKick.why: A chi-free spender, which is the thing this list is permanently short of. The proc lasts 15 seconds, so there is no hurry — and no reason to let it lapse either.

fistsOfFury.name: Fists of Fury
fistsOfFury.test: energy will not cap, and no brew or proc says hold
fistsOfFury.when: energy will not cap during the channel, you are not inside an Energizing Brew unless Rushing Jade Wind covers the whole of it, and — if a Re-Origination proc is running — the proc outlasts the channel and a brew is already up.
fistsOfFury.why: The most damage chi can buy, and four seconds doing nothing else — your auto-attacks are held for the whole channel too. All three conditions exist to stop those four seconds swallowing something.

tigerPalmProc.name: Tiger Palm
tigerPalmProc.test: a free palm, past the opener, with room to spend it
tigerPalmProc.when: Combo Breaker has made it free, the opener is over, no Energizing Brew is running, and either the proc is nearly gone or energy is two globals from full.
tigerPalmProc.why: The same free-global logic as the kick, several rungs lower. Tiger Palm hits for very little, so a free one only earns its global when there is nothing better to put in it.

jab.name: Jab
jab.test: two or more chi below the cap
jab.when: you are two or more chi below the cap.
jab.why: Two below, not one. Jab returns two chi, so pressing it one short of the cap throws the second away. Everything above it spends what this generated.

rushingJadeWind.name: Rushing Jade Wind
rushingJadeWind.test: energy is a second from capping, or the pull is under 75s
rushingJadeWind.when: energy is a second or less from capping. The other half of the condition compares the whole pull's length against 75 seconds rather than the time elapsed, so on any longer pull it is false from the first global to the last, and only the energy check remains.
rushingJadeWind.why: 40 energy on a six-second cooldown, and down here it is no longer free filler. Past 75 seconds this rung fires only to stop the bar overflowing, so the 40 it costs is energy that was about to be thrown away. At two targets the rung near the top takes over instead.

blackoutKick.name: Blackout Kick
blackoutKick.test: 35 energy still banked when the kick returns
blackoutKick.when: you will still have 35 energy banked by the time Rising Sun Kick comes back.
blackoutKick.why: The chi dump, and the only entry that looks ahead. Spending chi here is right only if what is left still covers the Jabs the next Rising Sun Kick needs.

stormEarthAndFire.name: Storm, Earth and Fire
stormEarthAndFire.test: one clone at 2 targets, two at 3+
stormEarthAndFire.when: two targets, for one clone. Three or more, for two.
stormEarthAndFire.why: A clone cuts everyone's damage, yours included: to 60% each with one out, 45% each with two. One clone across two enemies is 120% of your damage, two across three is 135%. At one enemy there is nowhere to put a clone, so it is pure loss and the list never casts it.

rushingJadeWindMulti.name: Rushing Jade Wind
rushingJadeWindMulti.test: the dot is not already spinning
rushingJadeWindMulti.why: It moves above Rising Sun Kick. The wind hits everything for as long as it spins and the kick hits one, so the second enemy is roughly where they cross. From three it returns a chi as well.

spinningCraneKick.name: Spinning Crane Kick
spinningCraneKick.why: It moves above Fists of Fury. Fists splits one lump evenly across everything in front of you, so its total never grows with the pack; this one's does. Three is where the growing one passes the fixed one.

blackoutKickDump.name: Blackout Kick
blackoutKickDump.test: 105 energy still banked when the kick returns
blackoutKickDump.when: 105 energy will still be banked by the time Rising Sun Kick comes back, rather than 35.
blackoutKickDump.why: With Spinning Crane Kick in the list there is far more worth spending energy on, so the chi dump has to leave three times as much behind before it fires.

craneOverKick.name: Spinning Crane Kick
craneOverKick.test: the kick's debuff is safe for another 2.25 seconds
craneOverKick.when: four targets and up, with the Rising Sun Kick debuff safe for another 2.25 seconds.
craneOverKick.why: Now it goes above Rising Sun Kick as well. The 2.25 seconds is what keeps the debuff from being lost to it: at four targets the kick is delayed, not dropped.

risingSunKickMulti.name: Rising Sun Kick
risingSunKickMulti.when: nothing above it fired. No condition at all, and at one enemy this is the kick's only rung — the one above it needs a second target — so it lands here, after Tiger Palm's refresh. From three it is where the kick lands once the pack has pushed it off that rung, and from four after Spinning Crane Kick as well.
risingSunKickMulti.why: It never leaves the list, because the debuff lifts everything else you press. Nothing drops the kick — the refresh above it, and from three the pack buttons, only delay it.

notes.snapshot: Tigereye Brew reads your mastery once, when the buff goes up, and never again. That is why the priority list spends it on the last global of a Re-Origination proc: the proc's ten seconds of converted stats are frozen into a fifteen-second buff and carried on after the proc has gone.
notes.channel: Nothing else in the list is read while Fists of Fury channels — not a brew, not a cooldown, not the debuff. Four seconds is long enough for a cooldown to come up, a proc to land and the debuff to fall off with nothing done about any of them.
notes.debuff: Rising Sun Kick's debuff goes on every enemy, not just the one you kicked, and lifts all your abilities by 20% for fifteen seconds — auto-attacks aside. Losing it costs a sixth of that, across the whole pack, for as long as it is down.
notes.talents: The list assumes two talent choices and skips the entries you did not take. Rushing Jade Wind and Invoke Xuen share a row, so you can never have both — which is why they are two rungs above rather than a fork. Chi Wave, Zen Sphere and Chi Burst share a row too, drawn as a fork wherever this log cannot tell which you brought.
notes.inferred: A rung only leaves the flow above on proof that the button was not on your bar. A log carries no talent tree, so a button you never pressed is exactly the one you may have forgotten — an unpressed rung is never removed. What is removed is the alternative to something you did press: a Spinning Crane Kick rules out Rushing Jade Wind, and a Chi Wave settles the row it shares with Zen Sphere and Chi Burst.
notes.mastery: One correction, because the name misleads. Your mastery in this patch is Bottled Fury, and all it does is make each Tigereye Brew stack hit harder. There is no alternating-ability mastery here — Combo Strikes belongs to a later expansion — so pressing the same button twice in a row costs you nothing.
notes.jadeWind: Rushing Jade Wind is on the list twice, and the two are not alternatives. Entry 17 lifts it above Rising Sun Kick as soon as there is a second enemy and tests nothing else. Entry 31 keeps it near the bottom, where it sits at one target, and there it fires only with energy a second from capping or on a pull under 75 seconds. It costs 40, the same as a Jab, and returns one chi where Jab returns two — so the higher rung deliberately spends generator energy on the spinning area damage, while the lower one only fires when that energy was about to overflow anyway. Its own six-second cooldown, re-armed to whatever is left of the dot, keeps that from being every global.

takeaways.title: Key improvements
takeaways.clean: Nothing came out below its target, so there is no short list to give you. The sections below have the details.

snapshotRate.label: Catch the procs
snapshotRate.fix: You brewed on the last global of {{value, percent}} of your Re-Origination windows. Aim for {{target, percent}} — brewing one global early loses the proc's strongest seconds.

priority.title: Priority list
priority.intent: Every other section measures one thing on its own. This one walks the priority list alongside your pull and asks, at each global you spent: was a better button available right then?

priority.noResources: This log carried no energy or chi readings, so there is no bar to reconstruct and no way to tell what you could afford at each global. Nothing is judged here.
priority.forced_single: You are reading this pull as one target, so every press below is judged against the single-target order — including the stretches where the log counted more enemies.
priority.forced_multi: You are reading this pull as multi-target, so every press below is judged at three targets: Rushing Jade Wind and Spinning Crane Kick move up, Rising Sun Kick gains a rung above Tiger Palm, and Blackout Kick needs a much fuller bar.
priority.caption: Buttons that were available and passed over, most often first
priority.scope: The ladder covers the filler priorities — Rising Sun Kick downwards, the entries that decide what a global is spent on. Touch of Death is out because its condition is the target's health, which this report does not fetch; the cooldowns are out because each has its own section. A button you could not afford is never counted as passed over.

priority.reconstructed: Nothing here is graded, and this is why. WarcraftLogs only reports your chi when you spend it — about one press in six — so the chi behind these judgements is reconstructed by walking the log forward through what each button gains and costs. Against the readings it did not use, that walk is right 87–95% of the time. It is close but not perfect: a press judged against a bar that is off by one chi can be called a miss when it was not.

jadeWind.title: Rushing Jade Wind
jadeWind.intent: At one target, Invoke Xuen is the better level-90 choice and Rushing Jade Wind is a damage loss: its 40 energy buys one chi where a Jab buys two. It is worth a single-target press only when that energy would otherwise hit the cap and be lost, or on a pull shorter than 75 seconds. From two enemies up, it is your area damage and should be kept spinning — taking it removes Spinning Crane Kick from your bars.
